oneLineAnswer: A prescription drug given under the skin to shorten OFF episodes in advanced Parkinson's disease.
whatItIs: Apomorphine is a prescription medicine, not a supplement. It is a non-ergoline dopamine agonist, which means it acts like dopamine, a chemical your brain uses to control movement. Chemically it is a small molecule with the formula C17H17NO2. The approved products are given under the skin, and they are used only in people with advanced Parkinson's disease.
whatItDoes: It is meant to shorten OFF episodes, the stretches when Parkinson's movement symptoms come back between doses of levodopa.
It is added to other Parkinson's medicines, mainly levodopa, rather than replacing them.
It works by stimulating dopamine receptors in the brain, although the label says the exact reason it helps is not known.
In one 12 week trial, people using an apomorphine infusion cut their daily OFF time more than people given a placebo.
It is not sold or studied as a general wellness product for people without Parkinson's disease.
howPeopleUseIt: One approved form is a continuous infusion under the skin through a small pump, running through the waking day, with extra doses for OFF episodes as needed.
An earlier injected form was given as a single dose under the skin when an OFF episode started.
A clinician sets the dose and is the only one who changes it.
Many people also take an antiemetic, a medicine that eases nausea and vomiting, when they first start.

commonSideEffects: A lump or nodule where the infusion goes in. The main trial recorded this in about 44 of every 100 people using the pump.
Redness at the infusion site, recorded in about 17 of every 100 people in that trial.
Nausea and vomiting, which can be severe.
Dyskinesia, meaning sudden movements you cannot control.
Headache and trouble falling or staying asleep.
Dizziness, low blood pressure, weakness, fatigue, and constipation.
seriousSigns: Falling asleep without warning while eating, talking, or driving.
Fainting, or dizziness when you stand up, caused by low blood pressure.
Falls, including serious ones with broken bones.
An infection at the infusion site, such as cellulitis.
Hallucinations, that is seeing or hearing things that are not there, plus confusion or agitation.
New or much stronger urges to gamble, spend money, or have sex that you cannot control.
Chest pain, shortness of breath, or a fast or irregular heartbeat. Heart attacks and sudden death have been reported with apomorphine injections.
Signs of low red blood cells (hemolytic anemia) such as looking pale, unusual tiredness, yellow skin or eyes, or dark urine.

An allergic reaction: hives, rash, swelling of the eyes, tongue, lips, or mouth, or trouble breathing. The injection contains a sulfite, which can trigger reactions in some people, especially those with asthma.
An erection that lasts more than 4 hours (priapism).
Blood clots if the liquid is accidentally put into a vein instead of under the skin.
whoShouldAvoid: Anyone taking an anti-nausea drug of the 5HT3 type, such as ondansetron. Very low blood pressure and blackouts have been reported with that combination, so it is not allowed.
Anyone allergic to apomorphine or to sulfites. The injection contains sodium metabisulfite.
Children. The label says safety and effectiveness have not been established in children.
People with a major psychotic disorder, because the drug can make psychosis worse, need to discuss it with a clinician first.
People with low blood pressure, fainting spells, daytime sleepiness, heart problems, kidney or liver problems, or asthma are told to raise these with a clinician before starting.

interactions: 5HT3 anti-nausea drugs (ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron) and alosetron must not be taken with apomorphine.
Blood pressure medicines and vasodilators, which are drugs that widen blood vessels, raise the risk of low blood pressure, falls, and injuries.
Nitroglycerin taken under the tongue causes a larger drop in blood pressure.
Alcohol causes a larger drop in blood pressure, and the label tells people not to drink while using apomorphine.
Antipsychotic drugs and metoclopramide can make apomorphine work less well.
Trimethobenzamide, often given for nausea, adds to sleepiness, dizziness, and falls.
Other medicines that affect the heart's electrical rhythm need caution, because apomorphine can stretch the QT interval.
Levodopa levels in the body are not changed when apomorphine is given at the same time.
pregnancyAndChildren: There are no adequate human data on apomorphine use in pregnancy. Animal studies found harm to developing animals, and the label says the drug may harm a fetus. It is not known whether apomorphine passes into breast milk or how it would affect a breastfed baby. Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established.
whatWeDoNotKnow: No source we checked says apomorphine changes the course of Parkinson's disease, rather than easing OFF episodes.
Whether apomorphine passes into human breast milk, or affects a breastfed baby, is unknown.
The pregnancy findings come from animals. No human studies confirm or rule out the same risk in people.
Studies have not been done in people with severe kidney problems or severe liver problems.
Whether this type of dopamine agonist can cause the tissue changes in the pelvis, lungs, and heart valves seen with older ergot-derived drugs is unknown.
The meaning of the retinal damage seen in albino rats given apomorphine has not been established for people.
We found no public source describing a supplement use, a natural health use, or a use in people without Parkinson's disease.

evidence.publisher: openFDA, U.S. Food and Drug Administration (ONAPGO label)
evidence.claim: Apomorphine is approved to treat motor fluctuations in adults with advanced Parkinson's disease.
evidence.quote: ONAPGO is indicated for the treatment of motor fluctuations in adults with advanced Parkinson's disease.

evidence.publisher: openFDA, U.S. Food and Drug Administration (ONAPGO label)
evidence.claim: It acts on dopamine receptors, but the label states the exact mechanism is unknown.
evidence.quote: The precise mechanism of action of ONAPGO as a treatment for Parkinson's disease is unknown

evidence.publisher: openFDA, U.S. Food and Drug Administration (ONAPGO label)
evidence.claim: The most common side effects in the trial were infusion site nodule, nausea, somnolence, infusion site erythema, dyskinesia, headache, and insomnia.
evidence.quote: were infusion site nodule, nausea, somnolence, infusion site erythema, dyskinesia, headache, and insomnia

evidence.publisher: openFDA, U.S. Food and Drug Administration (ONAPGO label)
evidence.claim: Combining apomorphine with 5HT3 anti-nausea drugs is contraindicated.
evidence.quote: Using concomitant 5HT 3 antagonists, including antiemetics (e.g., ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron) and alosetron

evidence.publisher: openFDA, U.S. Food and Drug Administration (ONAPGO label)
evidence.claim: A 12 week trial found a statistically significant drop in daily OFF time versus placebo.
evidence.quote: There was a statistically significant reduction in the amount of daily OFF time in patients treated with ONAPGO compared to placebo

evidence.publisher: openFDA, U.S. Food and Drug Administration (ONAPGO label)
evidence.claim: Animal studies showed developmental harm, so the label warns of possible fetal harm.
evidence.quote: In animal reproduction studies, apomorphine had adverse developmental effects in rats (increased neonatal deaths) and rabbits (increased incidence of malformation)

evidence.publisher: openFDA, U.S. Food and Drug Administration (ONAPGO label)
evidence.claim: Safety and effectiveness in children are not established.
evidence.quote: Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established.

evidence.publisher: openFDA, U.S. Food and Drug Administration (apomorphine hydrochloride injection label)
evidence.claim: An earlier injectable apomorphine product was approved for intermittent treatment of OFF episodes alongside other Parkinson's medicines.
evidence.quote: indicated for the acute, intermittent treatment of hypomobility

evidence.publisher: PubChem, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
evidence.claim: PubChem records the same indication: acute, intermittent treatment of OFF episodes in advanced Parkinson's disease.
evidence.quote: Apomorphine is indicated to treat acute, intermittent treatment of hypomobility, off episodes associated with advanced Parkinson's disease.

evidence.publisher: PubChem, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH), quoting LiverTox
evidence.claim: A LiverTox summary carried by PubChem says apomorphine has not been linked to liver injury.
evidence.quote: it has not been associated with serum enzyme elevations during treatment nor has it been implicated in cases of acute liver injury

evidence.publisher: PubChem, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
evidence.claim: Apomorphine is a small molecule with formula C17H17NO2 and molecular weight 267.32.

evidence.claim: A phase 3 long-term safety study of apomorphine infusion is registered.

gaps: NCCIH has no apomorphine page. The URL https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/apomorphine returned 404, so no NCCIH content was used.
MedlinePlus drug monographs were excluded on purpose. NLM states they are American Society of Health-System Pharmacists content and copyrighted.

openFDA searches by brand name for APOKYN and KYNMOBI returned no label records. The current DailyMed name search lists ONAPGO and an older APOKYN entry, and does not list a sublingual film product, so no current sublingual apomorphine product is described here.
No LiverTox page was fetched directly. The LiverTox summary is reported only through its excerpt on the PubChem record that was fetched.
No human pregnancy data, no breast-milk data, and no pediatric data were found in any fetched source.
No fetched source describes a use in healthy people, a wellness use, or a supplement use.
The general openFDA apomorphine search returned mostly homeopathic products that list apomorphine as a trace ingredient. Those are unrelated to the prescription drug described here.
summary: This record covers what apomorphine is, how its approved under-the-skin forms are used for OFF episodes in advanced Parkinson's disease, its recorded side effects and drug interactions, and the gaps in what is known.
